extracted.intended_audience: corporate communicators and public relations professionals who write press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for PR practitioners on crafting press releases using journalism techniques — structuring releases as usable news stories, achieving clarity on complex topics, and applying storytelling strategies reporters use. Emphasizes writing that reporters can reuse and that serves the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the press release as a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The object of a press release is a news story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the release as a story rather than as promotional copy — adopt newsy structure and priorities so the output functions like something a reporter can turn into a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use language reporters can use (avoid forcing rewrites)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The release should be in language that reporters can use rather than rewrite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write copy that is immediately usable: clear sentences, proper attribution, usable facts and quotes, and minimal PR spin so reporters don’t need to rework or decode the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grab attention of time-pressed reporters with clear, creative writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicators are more likely to grab the attention of time-pressed reporters with clear, creative writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and creativity in leads and key points to break through reporters’ inbox overload; be concise and interesting to merit their limited time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think like a reporter: know what you must tell and what’s nice-to-have
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reporters have a list, sometimes only in their heads, of what they need to tell the story and what would be nice to have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, create the reporter’s checklist: essential facts (who, what, when, where, why, how), supporting data, and optional color — place essentials up front and make nice-to-have items clearly secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling purpose: capture experience, not just convey information
rubrics_metrics.description: “The purpose of a story is not to convey information but to capture experience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to help the reader/viewer/listener feel what it’s like to be there; avoid treating storytelling as merely narrative labeling — use sensory and scene-based techniques to evoke experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use details that define character
rubrics_metrics.description: Use details that define character as part of storytelling strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete, specific details (people’s actions, traits, context) that make sources and subjects vivid and human for readers, rather than abstract descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver action in a sequence of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Action should be delivered in a sequence of scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure narrative elements so events unfold in an understandable sequence rather than as isolated facts; this helps reporters and audiences follow causality and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dialogue over simple quotes or sound bites
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dialogue, rather than simple quotes or sound bites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quotes that reveal character, context, or a scene; avoid boilerplate or empty platitudes that add little reportage value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a purposeful variety of points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a purposeful variety of points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple perspectives (e.g., affected individuals, experts, organizational spokespeople) to enrich the story and give reporters usable angles and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for civic clarity when writing about complex topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Clark’s first section, “Civic Clarity,” tackles basic problems including writing about complex topics — making the message understandable when stories are packed with details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify and prioritize when topics are complex: strip extraneous detail, explain jargon, and organize information so the central message remains clear for the public and reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary loyalty to the public — prioritize public interest over employer spin
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you are writing as a representative of any significant institution, your first loyalty has to be to the public, and not to your employer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a public-first ethic: craft communications that serve public understanding and civic purposes (health, community, education, safety, self-governance, democracy) rather than mere corporate promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a broad readership (public writers beyond journalists)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is written for a wider audience — 'public writers' include journalists, researchers, scholars, speech writers, or advocates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple audiences beyond the media; make language accessible to non-specialists and stakeholders who also consume press materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid packing releases with so many details the message is lost
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate communicators often pack stories with so many details the message is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and edit ruthlessly: remove extraneous facts and jargon that obscure the central point, so the release communicates a single clear takeaway for reporters and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model writing on diverse, real-world examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Clark illustrates with examples from a wide range of sources (e.g., COVID-19 test instructions, New Yorker, The Atlantic, museum guides, student news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study diverse exemplars of good writing — not just PR materials — to learn techniques that make releases more usable and engaging for reporters and readers.
